addressed_problems.content: The paper identifies that the current iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) algorithm for finding winning tickets in media recommender systems requires a costly train-prune-retrain process repeated over many iterations, which limits the practical benefits of the approach. Future work should develop more efficient identification schemes that reduce the computational overhead of the search while still reliably discovering sparse sub-networks (winning tickets) that can achieve comparable or better recommendation performance than the full embedding table, thereby making the method feasible for large-scale industrial deployment.

Real-world recommender systems rely on implicit feedback interaction records, which often contain noisy or accidental interactions (e.g., a user clicking on an uninterested item). The paper notes that such noisy data can mislead model learning and that the huge number of interaction records leads to expensive training costs. An open problem is how to find winning tickets that are robust to this label noise and can efficiently handle large-scale implicit feedback datasets, ensuring that the identified sparse sub-networks maintain high recommendation accuracy despite the presence of spurious interactions.

The method presented in the paper operates in a transductive setting: pruning is performed on the entire user-item embedding matrix, which does not naturally generalize to new-coming users or items that were not seen during training. This limitation prevents the direct application of the lottery ticket hypothesis to dynamic, real-world recommendation environments where new users and items continuously appear. Future work should explore inductive pruning and sparse-embedding schemes that can produce winning tickets capable of handling unseen users/items, enabling the benefits of sparse embeddings to be extended to cold-start scenarios.

Media recommender systems represent each user and each item by a dense embedding vector and fit user-item interactions using these embeddings. In large-scale industrial settings the embedding table can contain millions to hundreds of millions of parameter vectors (for example, millions of items with 256-d embeddings), producing prohibitive memory footprints and slow inference. At the same time, users and items have heterogeneous interaction histories and informativeness, yet conventional practice assigns a uniform embedding dimension to all users and items; this uniformity amplifies over-parameterization and overfitting because many embeddings contain redundant or uninformative components. Sparse pruning methods can reduce embedding size but traditionally require training a large dense model first and then pruning, which incurs large training cost and limits deployment benefits. The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) suggests that dense networks contain small sparse sub-networks ("winning tickets") that can be trained from the same initialization to match dense performance; however, prior LTH work has been demonstrated primarily in vision and NLP and has not established whether such winning tickets exist for the core parameter of recommender systems—the user-item embedding table—nor whether practical pruning/search procedures can find them while giving real memory, inference, and training cost benefits in recommender settings. Consequently, there is a concrete methodological and empirical gap: recommender systems need methods that (a) identify sparse embedding sub-matrices that can be trained independently from initialization to match or exceed full-model recommendation accuracy, (b) do so without incurring prohibitive search/training overhead, and (c) yield quantifiable reductions in memory, inference complexity, and training time appropriate for large-scale media recommendation deployments.

nodes.content: In large-scale recommendation, practitioners require a principled statement of whether a dense user-item embedding matrix contains a much smaller sparse sub-matrix that can be trained from the same initialization to reach comparable ranking performance. Prior to this work, LTH had been demonstrated in CV and NLP but lacked a recommender-specific formalization and empirical validation: recommendation models use bipartite user-item graphs, BPR-style ranking losses, and sometimes graph convolutional neighborhood aggregation (e.g., LightGCN), and it was unknown whether a sparse sub-matrix of the embedding table could satisfy the same train-from-initialization property. Without such verification, engineers cannot rely on sparse-from-scratch training to reduce embedding scale, and there is no empirical basis for designing embedding-pruning pipelines that preserve ranking accuracy. The gap prevents confident adoption of LTH-style compression in recommender pipelines and leaves open whether embedding-specific structures (heterogeneous sparsity per user/item, graph aggregation) change LTH’s applicability.

Finding sparse embedding sub-matrices that can be trained from scratch requires a concrete search algorithm. Prior sparse-pruning practice either (1) trains a full dense model and prunes once (OMP) or (2) prunes randomly (RP), both of which may miss trainable sparse initializations or yield unstable results in ranking tasks. A reliable, repeatable algorithmic procedure is needed that (i) searches the combinatorial space of embedding-sparsity patterns progressively, (ii) preserves the initialization-dependent trainability property (rewinding), and (iii) outperforms naive baselines in both sparsity achieved and ranking metrics. Without such an algorithmic baseline, claims of sparse-from-scratch trainability in recommender systems would lack operational utility and reproducibility.

Practitioners can choose among multiple embedding compression techniques (dense low-rank or transformed compressed embeddings like LCM; dynamic threshold sparse pruning like PEP; or train-from-scratch sparse sub-networks hypothesized by LTH). Before this work, it was unclear which approach gives the best ranking accuracy for a given parameter budget in media recommendation. Dense compression (LCM) preserves uniform embedding dimensionality but cannot adapt per-user/item capacity; trainable sparse methods (PEP) incorporate dynamic thresholds but require hyperparameter tuning. A head-to-head empirical comparison is necessary to determine whether LTH-style winning tickets are competitive with or superior to these alternatives in terms of recommendation metrics and stability. Without such comparisons, system designers cannot justify choosing LTH-based sparse embeddings over existing compression approaches.

Reducing embedding parameters is only useful if it leads to concrete reductions in inference time and memory cost under realistic recommender workloads. Prior to this analysis, it was not explicitly characterized how per-node sparse embeddings (heterogeneous sparsity across users/items) map to asymptotic time and memory complexities in standard recommender inference routines (dot-product scoring and, for graph models, neighborhood aggregation). Without such formulas and definitions of $F_u^*$ and $F_i^*$, claims about computational advantages of sparse embeddings remain qualitative and do not guide system-level resource planning or motivate storage/compute optimizations for sparse embedding representations.

Even if a sparse sub-matrix can match dense performance, its practical value depends on training cost. If training the sparse model from scratch requires as many epochs as the dense model, overall computational savings may be negated. Therefore, it is important to empirically measure whether winning tickets not only preserve accuracy but also reduce training-time budget. Without such measurements, practitioners cannot assess end-to-end cost trade-offs between dense and sparse-from-scratch workflows.

Applying IMP in practice requires choices (initial embedding dimension, per-iteration pruning rate, whether to rewind) that affect search effectiveness, efficiency, and stability. Absent empirical guidance, engineers may pick suboptimal $pr\\%$ or omit rewinding and thereby miss strong tickets or waste computation. A concise characterization of how these hyperparameters affect outcomes is needed to make LTH-MRS usable in production settings.

Beyond aggregate metrics, understanding which embedding components are pruned is important for interpretability and trust: practitioners need to know whether pruning removes random coordinates or selectively preserves salient signal. Without qualitative visualization and analysis, claims that IMP extracts "meaningful" sparse embeddings remain abstract and do not indicate whether pruning aligns with intuitive notions of feature importance.

Lottery Ticket Hypothesis for Media Recommender Systems (LTH-MRS) formalizes a winning-ticket condition on the user-item embedding table. For a recommender model $f(\mathcal{G};\boldsymbol{X})$ that takes as input a user-item bipartite graph $\mathcal{G}$ and a dense embedding table $\boldsymbol{X}$ (containing a vector of dimension $F$ for each user and item), and achieves test performance $a$ after $j$ epochs of training, let a binary mask $\mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{\|\boldsymbol{X}\|_0}$ define a sparse sub-matrix $\mathbf{M}\odot\boldsymbol{X}$, where $\|\boldsymbol{X}\|_0$ denotes the total number of parameters in $\boldsymbol{X}$. LTH-MRS requires the existence of a mask $\mathbf{M}$ such that when the model is trained from the same random initialization on the sub-matrix (i.e., $f(\mathcal{G};\mathbf{M}\odot\boldsymbol{X})$), it achieves test performance $a'$ after $j'$ epochs with $j'\le j$, $a'\ge a$, and $\|\mathbf{M}\|_0\ll\|\boldsymbol{X}\|_0$. Empirically, applying iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP), which repeatedly prunes the lowest-magnitude entries of the trained embedding table and rewinds the weights to the original initialization, to the user-item embedding table of Matrix Factorization (MF) and Light Graph Convolution Networks (LightGCN) on the Yelp2018, TikTok, and Kwai datasets produced sparse sub-matrices that, when trained from the original initialization, matched or exceeded the dense models' recommendation metrics. Specifically, for experiments with 32-dimensional embeddings, winning tickets were found that reduce the parameter count while achieving equal-or-better Recall at rank 20 (Recall@20) and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain at rank 20 (NDCG@20) compared to the full models.

metadata.narrative: The existence of winning tickets (Conclusion 1) rests primarily on the empirical results reported in Table 2 across three datasets and two models (H1 provides some generalization support). However, the central load‑bearing risk is the complete absence of statistical uncertainty quantification (P1): every reported metric is a single point estimate without any measure of dispersion. The small magnitude of some improvements (e.g., +0.0028 Recall@20 for MF on Yelp2018) could be within run‑to‑run noise, making it impossible to determine whether the “match or exceed” claim is genuine. H1 mitigates the risk that the finding is dataset‑specific but does not address the statistical uncertainty, which remains unprotected. The existence conclusion is therefore vulnerable at the quantitative magnitude and direction layers: if P1’s failure mode materializes, the foundational claim of LTH‑MRS is not reliably supported by the presented evidence.

nodes.title: Formalization of LTH-MRS and empirical existence of winning tickets in recommender embedding tables

nodes.content: The iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) procedure, where at each iteration the masked embedding table is trained for $J$ epochs, the lowest-magnitude $pr\%$ of remaining parameters are removed, and the remaining weights are rewound to their original random initialization, then repeated for $I$ iterations, stably identifies winning tickets in recommender embedding tables. Compared to Random Pruning (RP), which randomly removes elements from a trained embedding table, and One-shot Magnitude-based Pruning (OMP), which directly reduces a trained embedding table to the target sparsity based on element magnitude without iteration, IMP (with rewinding) (a) more reliably discovers tickets that preserve high sparsity while maintaining Recall at rank 20 (Recall@20); (b) yields quantitatively superior sparsity and accuracy. For Matrix Factorization (MF), IMP achieved improvements in the highest achievable sparsity over OMP by 30.8% (Yelp2018), 25.2% (TikTok), and 2.5% (Kwai), and improvements in highest Recall@20 by 18.8% (Yelp2018), 8.8% (TikTok), and 1.1% (Kwai). For Light Graph Convolution Networks (LightGCN), IMP improved highest sparsity over OMP by 22.0% (Yelp2018), 15.6% (TikTok), and 8.9% (Kwai), and improved highest Recall@20 by 6.6% (Yelp2018), 4.0% (TikTok), and 3.4% (Kwai). Random Pruning (RP) failed to stably find winning tickets in most settings.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2 (IMP reliably identifies winning tickets and outperforms RP and OMP) is supported by consistent improvements across all six dataset×model combinations (H2), which provides strong quantitative evidence that IMP’s advantage is not coincidental. However, the comparison suffers from a potentially asymmetric evaluation protocol (P2): it is unclear whether RP and OMP were also rewound to the original initialization before retraining, as IMP is. If they were not, the reported margins (e.g., 30.8% improvement in sparsity) could be partially or entirely artifactual, because a fair comparison would require all methods to perform the same task of finding trainable‑from‑scratch sub‑networks. P2 is the dominant risk: it threatens the comparative ranking layer. H2’s consistency is impressive but cannot compensate for a flawed protocol. The conclusion is therefore highly uncertain, with H2 providing some residual confidence but insufficient to overcome the fairness concern.

nodes.title: IMP reliably identifies winning tickets and outperforms alternative pruning strategies

nodes.content: Sparse embedding sub-matrices discovered by iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP, i.e., winning tickets) yield higher ranking accuracy than two representative embedding-compression baselines under matched parameter budgets: Linear Compression Model (LCM), which compresses the dense embedding table into a small dense matrix with trainable feature transformation, and Plug-in Embedding Pruning (PEP), which prunes the embedding table into a small sparse matrix using a trainable dynamic pruning threshold. For Light Graph Convolution Networks (LightGCN) on the Yelp2018 dataset with a 128-dimensional original embedding, the winning ticket improves Recall at rank 20 (Recall@20) and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain at rank 20 (NDCG@20) over LCM by 9.18% and 10.54% at 50% sparsity, and by 21.23% and 21.00% at 25% sparsity. Across all tested settings (multiple embedding dimensions and sparsity levels on the Yelp2018, TikTok, and Kwai datasets), winning tickets consistently obtain the best Recall@20 and NDCG@20 among the three methods with comparable parameter counts.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 3 (winning tickets outperform LCM and PEP) is supported by a systematic comparison across 12 settings (H3), which consistently shows superior metrics. This consistency across embedding dimensions, sparsity levels, and datasets provides strong evidence that the advantage is robust. The main risk is that hyperparameters for LCM and PEP may not have been independently tuned (P3), as the paper does not describe any tuning procedure for these baselines. However, the large and consistent margins (e.g., 21.23% improvement over LCM at 25% sparsity) suggest that even with optimal tuning, it is unlikely that the baselines would surpass winning tickets across all settings. P3 thus acts as a refinement risk rather than a show‑stopper: it may shift the magnitude of the advantage but is unlikely to flip the ranking. The comparative ranking layer is well‑supported by H3’s breadth, and the unprotected risk is moderate.

nodes.title: Winning tickets outperform embedding-compression baselines LCM and PEP

nodes.content: For dense Matrix Factorization (MF) with $M$ users, $N$ items, and embedding dimension $F$, the inference time complexity is $O(M\times N\times F)$ and memory complexity is $O(M\times F + N\times F)$. For a winning ticket represented by mask $\mathbf{M}$, define per-user masks $\mathbf{M}_u$ for user $u\in\mathcal{U}$ and per-item masks $\mathbf{M}_i$ for item $i\in\mathcal{I}$, where $\mathcal{U}$ is the set of users and $\mathcal{I}$ is the set of items. Let $F_u^* = \max_{u\in\mathcal{U}} \|\mathbf{M}_u\|_0$ be the maximum number of nonzero entries across all user masks, and $F_i^* = \max_{i\in\mathcal{I}} \|\mathbf{M}_i\|_0$ be the maximum number of nonzero entries across all item masks. Then MF inference time becomes $O\big(M\times N\times \min(F_u^*,F_i^*)\big)$ and memory becomes $O\big(M\times F_u^* + N\times F_i^*\big)$. For a $K$-layer Light Graph Convolution Network (LightGCN), the dense inference time complexity is $O\big(K\times \|\mathbf{A}\|_0 \times F + M\times N\times F\big)$ and memory complexity is $O(M\times F + N\times F)$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is the adjacency matrix of the user-item bipartite graph and $\|\mathbf{A}\|_0$ denotes the number of non-zero entries in $\mathbf{A}$. Replacing $F$ with $\min(F_u^*,F_i^*)$ in the neighborhood aggregation term $K\times \|\mathbf{A}\|_0 \times F$ and similarity computation term $M\times N\times F$ yields winning-ticket LightGCN inference time $O\big(K\times \|\mathbf{A}\|_0 \times \min(F_u^*,F_i^*) + M\times N\times \min(F_u^*,F_i^*)\big)$ and memory $O\big(M\times F_u^* + N\times F_i^*\big)$. These formulas demonstrate that when $F_u^*$ and $F_i^*$ are much smaller than $F$, both time and memory are substantially reduced.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 4 provides theoretical complexity formulas that are formally derived from the definitions of per‑node masks and the model operations (H5). The derivation is logically sound under the stated idealizations (linear scaling of dot product with min sparsity). No load‑bearing weak points were identified: the formulas are mathematical consequences of the definitions, not empirical claims requiring validation. The conclusion that time and memory are reduced when $F_u^*,F_i^* \ll F$ is a direct implication of the formulas. The prior probability is high because the derivation is straightforward and no uncertain bridges were found.

nodes.title: Theoretical complexity reductions for winning-ticket embeddings in MF and LightGCN

nodes.content: Empirically, winning tickets train markedly faster than full dense embedding tables to reach comparable recommendation performance. As measured in relative training epochs required to reach comparable performance, a 32-dimensional Matrix Factorization (MF) winning ticket reached comparable test metrics with roughly 1/8 the number of training epochs of the corresponding full embedding, representing an 8× faster effective learning speed. Similar relative speedups are observed across other tested settings.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 5 (winning tickets train faster in practice) is based on an epoch‑count comparison (Figure 6) without reporting wall‑clock times or defining “comparable performance” (P5). The measurement layer is weak: epochs are not a valid proxy for actual training time because per‑epoch cost may differ between masked and dense embeddings. No highlight was identified that addresses this measurement gap. The claim therefore rests on an incomplete and ambiguous metric. If P5’s failure mode materializes, the practical speedup claim would be unsupported. The conclusion has low credibility.

nodes.title: Winning tickets train faster in practice (empirical training-speedup)

nodes.content: Controlled ablations on iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) implementation choices yield the following conclusions. (a) Winning tickets exist for multiple original embedding sizes; across different original embedding dimensions $F$, the performance versus sparsity trends for lottery tickets are consistent, so IMP robustly finds tickets when varying $F$. (b) The iterative pruning rate $pr\%$ influences search: a lower $pr\%$ achieves higher best Recall at rank 20 (Recall@20), indicating more effective search, while a higher $pr\%$ reduces the number of pruning iterations needed to reach high sparsity, indicating more efficient search; the maximum sparsity achievable is similar across tested $pr\%$ values. (c) The rewinding mechanism, which resets weights to the original initialization after each pruning iteration, is necessary: IMP with rewinding finds winning tickets more stably and with higher Recall@20 and achievable sparsity than IMP without rewinding.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 6 contains three sub‑claims: (a) existence across original embedding sizes is well‑supported by Figure 3 across datasets and models; (b) the effect of iterative pruning rate is tested only on Yelp2018 with LightGCN (P6); (c) rewinding is necessary is tested only on Yelp2018 with LightGCN (P6) but with a controlled ablation that shows a clear benefit (H4). Sub‑claim (a) is strong and not threatened by P6. Sub‑claims (b) and (c) are supported only on one dataset–model pair, limiting their generality. H4 provides good support for (c) within that narrow setting, but the external validity remains unestablished due to P6. The overall conclusion about implementation insights is thus partially supported: the existence across sizes is robust, but the guidance on pruning rate and rewinding should be considered provisional until replicated on other datasets and models.

nodes.title: Ablation insights: original embedding size, iterative pruning rate, and rewinding matter

nodes.content: Visual inspection of a high-sparsity winning ticket, specifically the first ten users and ten items on the Yelp2018 dataset, shows that iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) tends to retain high-magnitude embedding components and prune low-magnitude (noisy or redundant) components, effectively denoising the embeddings. The sparse mask concentrates preserved coordinates at positions with larger absolute values in the original dense vectors.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 7 (winning tickets preserve high‑magnitude informative components) relies entirely on a qualitative visualization of 10 users and 10 items (P7). The sample is tiny and not quantitatively validated; no statistical measure links magnitude to survival probability across the embedding matrix. The conclusion is not supported by the evidence presented. No highlight was identified that could compensate for this anecdotal basis. The interpretability claim has very low credibility.

nodes.title: Winning tickets preserve high-magnitude (informative) embedding components (qualitative visualization)

nodes.content: In the evaluation of winning tickets on the Yelp2018, TikTok, and Kwai datasets using Matrix Factorization (MF) and Light Graph Convolution Networks (LightGCN) with 32-dimensional embeddings, each reported Recall at rank 20 (Recall@20) and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain at rank 20 (NDCG@20) value is a single point estimate without any measure of dispersion, such as standard deviation, confidence interval, or report across multiple random seeds. When the difference between the dense baseline metric and the winning ticket metric at a given sparsity is small (e.g., for MF on Yelp2018, the dense baseline Recall@20 was 0.0459 and the 27.1% sparsity winning ticket achieved 0.0487, a difference of 0.0028), it is impossible to determine whether the observed match or exceedance reflects a genuine systematic phenomenon or random variation arising from training stochasticity due to the Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) loss and negative sampling.

metadata.failure_mode: If the observed improvements are within the range of random variation, then the empirical claim that winning tickets exist (i.e., that there exists a mask satisfying a'≥a) is not reliably established for the tested configurations. A ticket that appears to match or exceed in a single run may actually underperform in expectation. The foundational existence claim of LTH-MRS would be unsupported by the presented evidence, undermining the entire empirical basis of the paper.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper provides no information about the number of independent runs, random seeds, or any measure of dispersion. In recommender system evaluation, it is standard practice (e.g., in SIGIR/RecSys papers) to report mean ± standard deviation over multiple seeds because BPR training with negative sampling introduces considerable stochasticity that can affect final ranking metrics by several percent. Without such reporting, the small observed differences cannot be reliably attributed to the winning ticket property rather than to noise. The magnitude of some improvements (e.g., ~2% relative for MF on Yelp2018) is comparable to typical run-to-run variation in such models.

nodes.title: Lack of statistical uncertainty quantification in winning-ticket evaluation

nodes.content: In the comparison of iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) with Random Pruning (RP) and One-shot Magnitude-based Pruning (OMP) on Yelp2018, TikTok, and Kwai datasets using Matrix Factorization (MF) and Light Graph Convolution Networks (LightGCN) with 32-dimensional embeddings, the evaluation protocol for RP and OMP is not fully specified. The definitions of RP as "randomly removes elements from a trained embedding table" and OMP as "directly reduce a trained embedding table to the target sparsity based on the element magnitude without iterations" do not explicitly state whether the resulting sparse sub-matrices are rewound to the original random initialization $\boldsymbol{X}^0$ (as IMP does) or retain the post-training parameter values before retraining. If RP and OMP are not rewound, the comparison is asymmetrical because IMP's rewinding is a known contributor to its success; consequently, the observed inferiority of RP and OMP may be partially or entirely due to this asymmetry rather than inherent inferiority of the pruning strategy.

metadata.failure_mode: If the evaluation is asymmetric, the conclusion that IMP “reliably finds winning tickets and outperforms alternative pruning strategies” may be overstated. The observed advantage (e.g., 30.8% improvement in highest sparsity for MF on Yelp2018) could shrink or disappear under a symmetric protocol. The comparative ranking of IMP versus RP and OMP would not be reliably established, weakening the operational guidance that practitioners should prefer IMP.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper’s methodological description for RP and OMP is insufficient. The original LTH literature defines winning tickets as sub‑networks trainable from the original initialization (rewinding). If RP and OMP are evaluated without rewinding (i.e., the pruned sub‑network retains the trained weights and is then fine‑tuned or retrained without resetting), they are not being asked to perform the same task: they merely prune a trained network, which is not a winning‑ticket search procedure. The paper later shows that rewinding is important (Figure 5), but the comparison with RP/OMP may have already baked in that advantage. A fair comparison would require either rewinding all methods to the same initial state or clearly stating the protocol and its implications.

nodes.title: Potential asymmetry in evaluation protocol between IMP and RP/OMP

nodes.content: In the comparison of winning tickets against Linear Compression Model (LCM) and Plug-in Embedding Pruning (PEP) on the Yelp2018, TikTok, and Kwai datasets using Light Graph Convolution Networks (LightGCN) with embedding sizes 64 and 128 at sparsity levels 50% and 75%, it is not stated whether the hyperparameters (learning rate, L2 regularization weight, training epochs, and for PEP the trainable pruning threshold and related hyperparameters) were independently optimized for LCM and PEP or kept at the default values used for the backbone models. Because LCM employs a different architecture (dense linear compression) and PEP uses its own dynamic pruning threshold, default hyperparameters are unlikely to be optimal for these methods. Consequently, the reported performance gaps, such as the 21.23% improvement in Recall at rank 20 (Recall@20) over LCM at 25% sparsity on Yelp2018, could partially reflect suboptimally tuned baselines rather than inherent superiority of winning tickets.

metadata.failure_mode: If the baselines are under‑tuned, the conclusion that winning tickets “yield higher ranking accuracy than … LCM and PEP” under matched parameter budgets may be inflated. Under fair tuning, the advantage could be smaller or reverse for some settings. The practical recommendation to use LTH‑style pruning over dense compression (LCM) or threshold‑based pruning (PEP) would be less strongly supported, reducing the paper’s contribution to embedding‑compression methodology.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper specifies hyperparameters for the backbone models (Adam, lr=0.001, λ=0.0001, batch size 2048, epochs 1000) but does not mention any tuning for LCM or PEP. LCM introduces a linear transformation matrix that may require different learning rates or regularization to avoid overfitting on small parameter counts. PEP uses a trainable threshold whose tuning, as the paper itself notes, “requires expensive time for tuning those hyperparameters carefully.” Without reporting the tuning procedure or resulting hyperparameters, it is unclear whether the comparisons are fair. The large margins (up to 21%) make it plausible that at least part of the gap is real, but the lack of transparency prevents confidence.

nodes.title: Unspecified hyperparameter tuning for compression baselines LCM and PEP

nodes.content: In the reported training speed comparison between winning tickets and the dense embedding baseline, the metric used is the relative number of training epochs required to reach "comparable performance". For example, a 32-dimensional Matrix Factorization (MF) winning ticket is said to reach comparable performance with 1/8 the training epochs of the dense embedding baseline. However, no wall-clock training times are reported, and the definition of "comparable performance" (e.g., matching the dense model's final test metric or reaching a fixed validation threshold) is not specified. Additionally, if each epoch of the winning ticket is computationally slower per parameter due to mask application, irregular memory access, or reduced GPU parallelism, the epoch-based speedup may not translate into actual time savings, potentially overstating the practical training benefit.

metadata.failure_mode: If the per‑epoch time for the winning ticket is substantially larger (e.g., 4× slower per epoch), the 8× epoch reduction could become only 2× wall‑clock speedup or even a slowdown. The conclusion that winning tickets “train markedly faster in practice” would not be supported by the presented evidence. Practitioners who adopt the method based on claimed time savings may not realize them, reducing the practical value of the finding.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper normalizes training epochs without considering per‑epoch computational cost. In practice, training a masked embedding table may be slower per epoch than a dense one because: (1) the binary mask must be applied in each forward pass; (2) the irregular sparsity pattern reduces the efficiency of GPU tensor cores; (3) gradient updates require scatter operations. Without reporting wall‑clock times or at least demonstrating that per‑epoch times are comparable, the claimed 8× speedup is at best a reduction in required optimization steps, not in actual training duration. Moreover, “comparable performance” is undefined, making the metric ambiguous and potentially irreproducible.

nodes.title: Training speed measured in epochs, not wall-clock time, without controlling per-epoch overhead

nodes.content: The ablation experiments for the iterative pruning rate (5%, 10%, and 20%) and for the rewinding mechanism were conducted only on the Yelp2018 dataset using Light Graph Convolution Networks (LightGCN). The conclusions drawn—that a lower pruning rate $pr\%$ yields higher best Recall at rank 20 (Recall@20), that a higher $pr\%$ reduces the number of pruning iterations, and that rewinding improves performance and stability—are not replicated on the TikTok or Kwai datasets or with the Matrix Factorization (MF) model. Therefore, the observed patterns may be specific to Yelp2018's interaction density and popularity distribution or to LightGCN's graph convolution properties, and may not generalize to other recommender settings.

metadata.failure_mode: If the ablation patterns are dataset‑specific, then the general recommendations that practitioners should use lower $pr\%$ for better accuracy and always apply rewinding may be suboptimal on other datasets (e.g., TikTok or Kwai). The conclusion that “IMP implementation choices … produce these conclusions” as general findings would be overclaimed because the evidence is insufficient to support their generality. The practical utility of the ablation insights would be limited to settings similar to Yelp2018 with LightGCN.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper uses Yelp2018 for these ablations, which has the highest interaction density (0.00130) among the three datasets. LightGCN with its aggregation and layer combination may respond differently to pruning rates than MF. Without validation on other datasets and models, the generality of the findings about $pr\%$ trade‑offs and rewinding necessity is unsubstantiated. The paper does not discuss why Yelp2018 was chosen or provide evidence that the patterns hold elsewhere.

nodes.title: Ablation studies on pruning rate and rewinding performed on Yelp2018 alone with LightGCN

nodes.content: The qualitative visualization of the winning ticket on the Yelp2018 dataset shows only the first 10 users and 10 items, with a visual comparison of retained versus pruned embedding components. The claim that iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) "tends to retain high-magnitude embedding components and prune low-magnitude (noisy or redundant) components" is based solely on this small, ad-hoc sample (20 out of approximately 70,000 nodes) without any quantitative metric such as the fraction of top-k magnitude entries preserved across the entire embedding matrix or a statistical test of magnitude-survival correlation. Therefore, the visual pattern may not generalize to the full dataset.

metadata.failure_mode: If the visual pattern does not generalize, the conclusion that winning tickets preserve high‑magnitude (informative) embedding components and effectively denoise embeddings is not supported by evidence. The interpretability insight would be little more than an anecdote, and the paper would not have demonstrated any meaningful understanding of which components are pruned.
metadata.weakness_reason: A sample of 10 users and 10 items out of 69,716 nodes is far too small to support a general claim about pruning behavior. Recommender system research has shown that visualization of a few examples can be misleading due to selection bias. The paper does not provide any quantitative analysis (e.g., rank‑correlation between absolute embedding value and survival probability, fraction of pruned components that are below the median of absolute values) that would substantiate the claim that pruning preserves informative components systematically.

nodes.title: Visualization of winning ticket components is anecdotal without quantitative analysis

nodes.content: The existence and effectiveness of winning tickets are demonstrated on three publicly available datasets (Yelp2018, TikTok, Kwai) that differ in domain (restaurant reviews vs short‑video platforms), size (7k–37k users, 38k–97k items), and interaction density (0.00021 to 0.00130). Winning tickets are found on all three datasets with both MF and LightGCN (Table 2, Figure 2), and the improvements over dense baselines are directionally consistent across datasets.

metadata.credit: This cross‑dataset replication preempts the threat that winning tickets might exist only on a particular interaction distribution or density regime. Without it, the conclusion that LTH holds for media recommender systems would rest on a single dataset, leaving doubt about generalizability. The diversity of the datasets (different domains, sizes, densities) provides moderate but real evidence that the phenomenon is not an artifact of one dataset. It underwrites the generalization layer of the conclusion: the existence claim is robust across the tested conditions, supporting the conclusion beyond a single‑dataset anecdote.

nodes.title: Multi‑dataset replication across three diverse real‑world datasets

nodes.content: Across 6 dataset×model pairs (MF and LightGCN on Yelp2018, TikTok, Kwai), IMP consistently improves over OMP in both highest achievable sparsity and highest Recall@20. For MF, the improvements in highest sparsity are 30.8% (Yelp2018), 25.2% (TikTok), 2.5% (Kwai); for LightGCN, 22.0%, 15.6%, 8.9%. All improvements are positive, with many being large relative to OMP’s absolute values. The pattern is systematic across all combinations (Section 4.3).

metadata.credit: The consistent directionality and substantial magnitude of IMP’s advantage over OMP across six independent evaluations significantly reduces the probability that the advantage is due to chance or to a single favorable configuration. If the advantage appeared in only one or two settings, it could be a fluke; the fact that it occurs in all six, with the largest improvements on the two denser datasets, provides quantitative support that IMP is more effective at finding winning tickets. This underwrites the comparative ranking layer of the conclusion: IMP is not just occasionally better but systematically outperforms OMP across diverse conditions.

nodes.title: Consistent and often large improvements of IMP over OMP across all dataset×model combinations

nodes.content: Table 3 reports Recall@20 and NDCG@20 for LightGCN on three datasets (Yelp2018, TikTok, Kwai) with two embedding sizes (64, 128) and two sparsity levels (50%, 75%), a total of 12 settings. In all 12 settings, winning tickets achieve the highest metric values, with margins over LCM ranging from ~2% to ~21% and over PEP from ~1% to ~10%. The consistency across dimensions and sparsity levels provides strong evidence that the advantage is not confined to a particular configuration.

metadata.credit: The full‑factorial design (embedding size × sparsity × dataset) addresses the threat of cherry‑picking a favorable configuration. If the comparison had been shown at only one size and one sparsity, one could argue that other settings might yield different rankings. By demonstrating superiority across 12 distinct configurations, the evidence strongly supports the conclusion that winning tickets generally outperform LCM and PEP under matched parameter budgets. This underwrites both the comparative ranking layer and the generalization of the advantage across dimensions and sparsity levels.

nodes.title: Systematic comparison across embedding dimensions and sparsity levels shows consistent superiority of winning tickets

nodes.content: On Yelp2018 with LightGCN, the paper compares IMP with rewinding versus IMP without rewinding (Figure 5). The results show that IMP with rewinding achieves higher Recall@20 across the sparsity range and reaches a higher maximum sparsity while maintaining acceptable performance. The two curves are clearly separated, and the advantage of rewinding persists across multiple pruning iterations.

metadata.credit: This controlled ablation directly tests the causal contribution of the rewinding mechanism. Without it, one could hypothesize that iterative pruning alone is sufficient and rewinding is irrelevant. The experiment provides empirical evidence that rewinding substantively improves both accuracy and achievable sparsity, preempting that alternative explanation. It underwrites the attribution layer of the conclusion: the success of IMP is at least partially attributable to rewinding, not just to iterative pruning. The scope of credit is limited to Yelp2018 with LightGCN, but within that setting the evidence is strong.

nodes.title: Controlled ablation study directly demonstrates the necessity and benefit of rewinding

nodes.content: The paper derives explicit formulas for inference time and memory complexity of winning‑ticket versions of MF and LightGCN. For MF: inference time $O(M \times N \times \min(F_u^*,F_i^*))$, memory $O(M \times F_u^* + N \times F_i^*)$. For LightGCN: inference time $O(K \times \|A\|_0 \times \min(F_u^*,F_i^*) + M \times N \times \min(F_u^*,F_i^*))$, memory $O(M \times F_u^* + N \times F_i^*)$, where $F_u^*$ and $F_i^*$ are the maximum per‑node embedding sizes after pruning (Section 3.5). These expressions are derived from the definitions of the models and the per‑node mask properties.

metadata.credit: The derivation provides precise, mathematically stated upper bounds on resource consumption in terms of the per‑node sparsity statistics. This preempts the ambiguity of vague “reduced complexity” claims, giving practitioners concrete formulas to estimate savings given actual sparsity distributions. The derivation is logically sound under the stated idealizations (linear scaling of dot product and aggregation with min of sparsities). It underwrites the quantitative potential claim of the conclusion: if $F_u^*,F_i^* \ll F$, then both time and memory are reduced in the asymptotic sense defined by these formulas.

nodes.title: Formal derivation of asymptotic complexity for winning‑ticket embeddings

steps.reasoning: State which upstream result is being used as given: the IMP algorithm's properties (that it stably identifies winning tickets and outperforms alternatives) established in the upstream result are treated as available and are used as the pruning/search mechanism for discovering candidate sparse embedding sub-matrices in recommender models.

Formalize the recommender model and embedding-table notation used in the winning-ticket definition: let $\mathcal{G}$ denote the user-item bipartite interaction graph, and let the recommender model be $f(\mathcal{G};\boldsymbol{X})$ where $\boldsymbol{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times F}$ is the user-item embedding table with $|\mathcal{V}|=M+N$ rows and embedding dimension $F$; denote by $\|\boldsymbol{X}\|_0$ the total number of scalar parameters in $\boldsymbol{X}$.

Introduce the binary mask and the sparse sub-matrix notation for formalizing LTH-MRS: let $\mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{\|\boldsymbol{X}\|_0}$ denote a binary mask over embedding parameters, and denote the masked/sparse embedding table by $\mathbf{M}\odot\boldsymbol{X}$ where $\odot$ is element-wise multiplication that zeroes pruned parameters.

Define the performance notation used in the winning-ticket condition: suppose the dense model $f(\mathcal{G};\boldsymbol{X})$ achieves best test performance $a$ after $j$ epochs of training, and suppose the masked model $f(\mathcal{G};\mathbf{M}\odot\boldsymbol{X})$ when trained from the same initialization achieves test performance $a'$ after $j'$ epochs. Explicitly define $a,a'$ as scalar test-performance measures (e.g., Recall@20 or NDCG@20) and $j,j'$ as integer epoch counts.

State the formal winning-ticket condition (the extension LTH-MRS): there exists a binary mask $\mathbf{M}$ such that $j'\le j$, $a'\ge a$, and $\|\mathbf{M}\|_0 \ll \|\boldsymbol{X}\|_0$. That is, a sparse sub-matrix $\mathbf{M}\odot\boldsymbol{X}$ can be trained from the same initialization to reach equal-or-better test performance in no more epochs while using far fewer parameters; such a sub-matrix is called a winning ticket in media recommender systems.
[11]

Describe the experimental instantiation used to verify LTH-MRS: apply the IMP search procedure (train masked model for $J$ epochs, prune lowest-magnitude $pr\%$, rewind to initialization, repeat $I$ iterations) to the user-item embedding tables of two backbone recommender models — Matrix Factorization (MF) and LightGCN — on three datasets (Yelp2018, TikTok, Kwai) to produce a sequence of sparse candidate sub-matrices $\{\mathbf{M}^1\odot\boldsymbol{X}^0,\mathbf{M}^2\odot\boldsymbol{X}^0,\ldots\}$, and then independently train each candidate from the original initialization to measure $a',j'$ for each.
Fig. 1

Report concrete empirical findings that establish the empirical existence of winning tickets: in the experiments with 32-dimensional embeddings, many sparse sub-matrices produced by IMP trained from the original initialization matched or exceeded the dense models' recommendation metrics (Recall@20 and NDCG@20) while drastically reducing parameter counts. For example, across datasets the winning tickets achieved the same or better performance using only between 29% and 48% of parameters on Yelp2018, 7% to 10% on TikTok, and 3% to 17% on Kwai, demonstrating wide existence of winning tickets in these media recommender systems.
Fig. 2

Cite specific example results from the experiments supporting the existence claim: for the Kwai dataset, a winning-ticket MF model improved Recall@20 by 28.7% and NDCG@20 by 35.5% while reducing parameters by 95.29%; for LightGCN on Kwai, a winning ticket improved Recall@20 by 10.0% and NDCG@20 by 7.99% while reducing parameters by 65.13%. These per-dataset/tabled numbers are reported in the paper's experimental results.
Fig. 2

Conclude that LTH-MRS is both formally defined and empirically verified: the formal condition (existence of mask $\mathbf{M}$ with $j'\le j$, $a'\ge a$, and $\|\mathbf{M}\|_0\ll\|\boldsymbol{X}\|_0$) constitutes LTH-MRS, and the experimental application of IMP to MF and LightGCN on Yelp2018, TikTok and Kwai produced sparse sub-matrices that satisfy this condition when trained from the original initialization, thereby empirically demonstrating that winning tickets exist in media recommender systems.
Table 2

State the pruning procedure used as a known algorithmic framework: iterative magnitude-based pruning (IMP) operates as follows — maintain a binary mask $\mathbf{M}\in\{0,1\}^{\|\boldsymbol{X}\|_0}$ over the embedding parameters, train the masked model $f(\mathcal{G};\mathbf{M}\odot\boldsymbol{X}^0)$ for $J$ epochs where $\boldsymbol{X}^0$ denotes the original random initialization, prune the lowest-magnitude $pr\%$ of remaining (non-zero) parameters by setting corresponding entries of $\mathbf{M}$ to $0$, rewind the dense weights to $\boldsymbol{X}^0$ (i.e., reset weights to original initialization), and repeat this train-prune-rewind loop for $I$ iterations to obtain progressively sparser masks and a set of candidate sparse sub-matrices. This procedure is the IMP algorithm as described in the methodology.
[11]
Fig. 1

Define the notation appearing in the algorithmic description: $\boldsymbol{X}^0$ is the randomly initialized dense user-item embedding table with $\|\boldsymbol{X}^0\|_0$ scalar parameters; $\mathbf{M}^i$ denotes the binary mask after $i$ pruning iterations; $pr\%$ denotes the iterative pruning rate (percentage of remaining non-zero parameters removed at each pruning step); $J$ denotes the number of training epochs performed on each masked model during the search; and $I$ denotes the total number of pruning iterations. The sparsity of $\mathbf{M}^i$ is $1-(1-pr\%)^{i}$ after $i$ iterations.

Treat the upstream experimental claim about IMP as available: the IMP procedure described above is used as the search method for candidate sparse embedding sub-matrices in the recommender models, and the experimental comparisons in the paper employ IMP (with rewinding), One-shot Magnitude-based Pruning (OMP), and Random Pruning (RP) as alternative pruning strategies applied to trained embedding tables; the experiments use backbone models Matrix Factorization (MF) and LightGCN on three datasets (Yelp2018, TikTok, Kwai) with 32-dimensional original embeddings and hyperparameters including $J=1000$, $pr\%=0.1$, and $I=30$. Treating these experimental settings as given, proceed to the empirical comparison results.
Fig. 2

Report the empirical observation that Random Pruning (RP) cannot stably find winning tickets: in the experiments, RP only managed to find winning tickets for LightGCN on the TikTok dataset, and otherwise failed to locate stable tickets. Relative to IMP and OMP, the winning tickets found by RP exhibited marked degradations: the RP-found tickets achieved declines of 40.7% and 27.3% in the highest sparsity and declines of 4.8% and 0.7% in the highest Recall@20 when compared respectively to IMP and OMP.
Fig. 2

Report the empirical observation that both IMP and OMP can find winning tickets but IMP yields superior results: the experiments show that IMP (with rewinding) identifies winning tickets more reliably and that the winning tickets produced by IMP consistently outperform those produced by OMP on both sparsity and accuracy metrics across datasets and backbone models.
Fig. 2

Provide the quantitative improvements of IMP over OMP for Matrix Factorization (MF): compared to OMP, IMP achieves improvements in the highest achievable sparsity for MF by 30.8% on Yelp2018, 25.2% on TikTok, and 2.5% on Kwai; and IMP achieves improvements in the highest Recall@20 for MF by 18.8% on Yelp2018, 8.8% on TikTok, and 1.1% on Kwai. These figures are reported from the experimental comparisons.
Fig. 2

Provide the quantitative improvements of IMP over OMP for LightGCN: compared to OMP, IMP achieves improvements in the highest achievable sparsity for LightGCN by 22.0% on Yelp2018, 15.6% on TikTok, and 8.9% on Kwai; and IMP achieves improvements in the highest Recall@20 for LightGCN by 6.6% on Yelp2018, 4.0% on TikTok, and 3.4% on Kwai. These values are reported in the experimental results comparing IMP and OMP.
Fig. 2

Synthesize the above experimental findings into the conclusion that IMP with rewinding is a stable and effective procedure for identifying winning tickets in recommender embedding tables: IMP's iterative train-prune-rewind loop preferentially removes low-magnitude embedding parameters while preserving or improving recommendation metrics when sparse sub-matrices are trained from the original initialization, and this empirical stability and superior sparsity/accuracy trade-off hold across backbone models (MF and LightGCN) and datasets (Yelp2018, TikTok, Kwai), whereas RP fails to stably find winning tickets in most settings.
Fig. 2

Start from the upstream result that LTH-MRS has been formalized and empirically established (the existence of winning tickets found by IMP on MF and LightGCN over Yelp2018, TikTok and Kwai) and treat those winning-ticket embeddings as available candidate compressed representations for comparison against other embedding-compression methods.

Define the two embedding-compression baselines used for comparison: (a) Linear Compression Model (LCM) compresses a large embedding table into a smaller dense matrix with a trainable feature transformation to represent users/items with uniform reduced-size dense vectors; (b) Plug-in Embedding Pruning (PEP) prunes the embedding table into a sparse matrix using a trainable dynamic pruning threshold mechanism. These baselines are experimentally implemented and compared to winning tickets under matched parameter budgets.
[10]

Describe the experimental comparison protocol: for LightGCN, compare Recall@20 and NDCG@20 of winning tickets discovered by IMP against LCM and PEP under equivalent parameter counts (i.e., matched effective parameter budgets) for multiple original embedding dimensions (e.g., 64 and 128) and multiple sparsity levels (e.g., 50% and 75%), then report the observed metric values to quantify relative performance.
Table 3

Present the concrete quantitative example from the experiments on Yelp2018 with LightGCN and a 128-dimensional original embedding: at 50% sparsity, the winning ticket achieves higher Recall@20 and NDCG@20 than LCM by 9.18% and 10.54%, respectively; at 25% sparsity the winning ticket improves Recall@20 and NDCG@20 over LCM by 21.23% and 21.00%, respectively. These percentage improvements are computed from the metric values reported in the comparison table.
Table 3

Report broader comparative trends across datasets and settings: across the reported settings (multiple embedding dimensions and sparsities on Yelp2018, TikTok, Kwai), winning tickets consistently obtain the best Recall@20 and NDCG@20 among the three methods (winning ticket, LCM, PEP) when parameter counts are comparable, indicating that the sparse sub-matrices discovered by IMP yield higher ranking accuracy than the representative dense-compression (LCM) and trainable-pruning (PEP) baselines under matched budgets.
Table 3

Explain the authors' interpretive reasoning for why winning tickets outperform LCM and PEP: as a dense compressed model that uses uniform-size embeddings, LCM cannot express per-node heterogeneity in informativeness and may underfit or over-parameterize users/items with differing popularity; by contrast, IMP-produced winning tickets (and PEP's dynamic-threshold pruning) adaptively allocate different effective embedding sizes to different users/items via pruning, thereby expressing heterogeneity and improving ranking metrics. This explanatory assertion is the authors' offered interpretation for the empirical superiority of winning tickets.

Conclude that the empirical evidence supports the assertion that winning tickets discovered by IMP outperform the two representative embedding-compression baselines (LCM and PEP) under matched parameter budgets, with the provided numerical examples substantiating the claim.

Define the dense Matrix Factorization (MF) setup and symbols: let $M$ denote the number of users, $N$ denote the number of items, and $F$ denote the embedding dimension (size of each user or item embedding vector). The dense user-item embedding table is $\boldsymbol{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{(M+N)\times F}$ where the first $M$ rows are user embeddings and the next $N$ rows are item embeddings.

State the dense MF inference and memory complexity formulas as derived in the paper: the dense MF inference time complexity is $O(M\times N\times F)$ because MF computes a score for every user-item pair by a dot product of $F$-dimensional vectors, and the memory complexity for storing embeddings is $O(M\times F + N\times F)$ to hold all user and item embeddings.

Introduce a winning-ticket mask structure and per-node masks: for a winning-ticket mask $\mathbf{M}\odot\boldsymbol{X}$, define $\mathbf{M}_u$ as the binary mask (vector) for user $u\in\mathcal{U}$ selecting preserved coordinates in user $u$'s embedding, and define $\mathbf{M}_i$ as the binary mask for item $i\in\mathcal{I}$. Define $F_u^*=\max_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\|\mathbf{M}_u\|_0$ as the maximum number of preserved (non-zero) coordinates across all users, and $F_i^*=\max_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\|\mathbf{M}_i\|_0$ as the maximum across items.

Derive MF inference and memory complexity when using the winning-ticket masks by observing that each dot product between a user and item embedding only needs to consider coordinates preserved in both vectors: the MF inference time complexity becomes $O\big(M\times N\times \min(F_u^*,F_i^*)\big)$ because for every user-item pair the effective vector length used in dot products is upper-bounded by $\min(F_u^*,F_i^*)$, and the memory complexity becomes $O\big(M\times F_u^* + N\times F_i^*\big)$ because at most $F_u^*$ coordinates are stored per user and $F_i^*$ per item.

Define the LightGCN setup and relevant symbols: let $\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{(M+N)\times(M+N)}$ denote the graph adjacency matrix of the user-item bipartite graph, $\|\mathbf{A}\|_0$ denote the number of non-zero entries (edges) in $\mathbf{A}$, and let $K$ denote the number of LightGCN layers. The base embedding dimension is $F$ as above.

State the dense LightGCN inference-time and memory complexities as given in the paper: the neighborhood aggregation across $K$ layers incurs $O\big(K\times\|\mathbf{A}\|_0\times F\big)$ time, the layer combination and embedding access incur $O(M\times F+N\times F)$ time, and the similarity computation (computing scores for all pairs) contributes $O(M\times N\times F)$. Considering $M+N\ll M\times N$, the overall dense LightGCN inference time is summarized as $O\big(K\times\|\mathbf{A}\|_0\times F + M\times N\times F\big)$ and memory is $O(M\times F + N\times F)$.

Apply the winning-ticket mask reductions to LightGCN by replacing $F$ with $\min(F_u^*,F_i^*)$ in the neighborhood aggregation and all similarity computations: the winning-ticket LightGCN inference time becomes $O\big(K\times\|\mathbf{A}\|_0\times \min(F_u^*,F_i^*) + M\times N\times \min(F_u^*,F_i^*)\big)$ and the memory complexity becomes $O\big(M\times F_u^* + N\times F_i^*\big)$.

Conclude the complexity reduction consequence: because winning tickets typically satisfy $F_u^*\ll F$ and $F_i^*\ll F$, replacing $F$ by $\min(F_u^*,F_i^*)$ yields substantial reductions in both inference time and memory compared to the dense models; therefore winning-ticket embeddings in both MF and LightGCN provide theoretical time and memory complexity benefits.

Start from the upstream result that winning tickets exist and can be trained independently from the original initialization (the LTH-MRS empirical finding) and that IMP is used to discover those tickets; treat those discovered winning tickets and their training runs as available experimental artifacts for measuring training speed.

Define the metric used to compare training speed: measure training speed as the relative number of training epochs required for a model to reach comparable test performance, where the consumed training epochs of a winning ticket are taken as one unit (i.e., normalized to 1) and the original dense embedding model's required epochs are reported relative to this baseline.

Report the empirical observations from the training-speed comparisons: the winning tickets consistently train markedly faster to reach a given recommendation performance than the full dense embedding tables; for example, the MF model with 32-dimensional embeddings produced a winning ticket that reached comparable test metrics with roughly one-eighth the number of training epochs of the corresponding full embedding table, corresponding to an 8× faster effective learning speed for that winning ticket.
Fig. 6

Generalize the empirical pattern: similar relative training-speedups (i.e., winning tickets requiring substantially fewer epochs than dense embeddings to reach comparable performance) are observed across other tested settings and datasets in the experiments, indicating that winning tickets can reduce the training cost in practice.
Fig. 6

Conclude that empirically, winning tickets train faster than their corresponding dense embedding tables, as quantified by the relative epoch counts (example: MF-32d winning ticket reached comparable performance with roughly 1/8 the epochs of the full model), demonstrating practical training-speedup benefits.

Begin from the upstream results that LTH-MRS is formalized and empirically validated (winning tickets exist) and that IMP is the search method used (IMP reliably finds winning tickets); treat those as given starting points for ablation analysis interpretation.

State the purpose of the ablation studies: to examine how implementation choices of IMP — original embedding size, iterative pruning rate $pr\%$, and the rewinding mechanism — affect the existence, quality, and search efficiency of winning tickets.

Effect of original embedding size: describe the experiment where IMP is run with different original embedding sizes (denoted by $F$ values such as 32, 64, 128) for the same backbone models and datasets; the reported observation is that for the same recommender model, lottery-ticket performance-vs-sparsity trends are almost consistent across different original sizes, and winning tickets are found robustly for all tested $F$ values, demonstrating that winning-ticket existence is not narrowly tied to a single original embedding size.
Fig. 3

Effect of iterative pruning rate $pr\%$: define $pr\%$ as the percentage of remaining non-zero parameters pruned at each IMP iteration; describe the experiment using different $pr\%$ values (5%, 10%, 20%) and report the observed trade-offs: (a) the highest sparsity achievable is approximately the same across tested $pr\%$ values; (b) lower $pr\%$ attains a higher best Recall@20 (i.e., more effective search quality), while (c) higher $pr\%$ requires fewer pruning iterations to reach high sparsity (i.e., more efficient search). These observations show $pr\%$ trades off search effectiveness and search efficiency.
Fig. 4

Effect of rewinding mechanism: define rewinding as resetting the pruned sub-network's dense weights after each pruning iteration back to the original initialization $\boldsymbol{X}^0$; describe the ablation comparing IMP with rewinding versus IMP without rewinding, and report the empirical findings: IMP with rewinding finds winning tickets more stably and reliably, and yields higher Recall@20 and higher achievable sparsity than IMP without rewinding. Therefore, rewinding is necessary for stable and effective winning-ticket identification in these experiments.
Fig. 5

Synthesize the ablation conclusions: (a) winning tickets exist across multiple original embedding sizes $F$ and IMP finds them robustly when $F$ varies; (b) $pr\%$ controls an effectiveness/efficiency trade-off — smaller $pr\%$ better search quality, larger $pr\%$ faster convergence to high sparsity while achieving similar maximum sparsity; (c) rewinding is essential for stability and higher performance in the IMP search procedure. These ablation insights inform practical choices of IMP hyperparameters.

Begin from the upstream result that winning tickets are discovered by IMP (winning tickets exist) and that specific high-sparsity tickets were obtained for case-study visualization; treat the identified winning-ticket masks and the original dense embeddings as available artifacts for inspection.

Describe the visualization experiment setup and notation: the authors visualized part of the original dense embedding table and an obtained highly sparse winning ticket on the Yelp2018 dataset by rendering the first 10 users and first 10 items; the visualization compares the per-coordinate magnitudes of the original dense vectors with the binary mask entries preserved by IMP to illustrate which coordinates are retained.
Fig. 7

Report the qualitative observation from the visualized example: the high-sparsity winning ticket produced by IMP tends to preserve coordinates in user and item embeddings that have larger absolute values in the original dense vectors and prune coordinates with low absolute values (interpreted as noisy or redundant), so the mask concentrates preserved coordinates at positions corresponding to larger-magnitude features, effectively removing low-magnitude noise.
Fig. 7

State the interpretive conclusion drawn from the visualization: by preferentially retaining higher-magnitude embedding components and pruning low-magnitude ones, IMP acts as a denoising mechanism on embeddings, producing sparse sub-matrices that maintain meaningful features while discarding redundancy—this qualitative pattern supports the authors' explanation of why winning tickets can preserve or improve recommendation performance despite drastic parameter reduction.

open_questions.content: The paper acknowledges several unresolved issues and directions for future research that limit immediate practical adoption: (1) Efficient identification: the IMP-based search requires repeated train-prune-retrain iterations (the costly iterative IMP procedure), so more efficient schemes for finding winning tickets are needed to make the approach practical at industrial scale. (2) Robustness to noisy implicit-feedback data: real recommender interaction logs contain many noisy or accidental implicit interactions; how to find winning tickets that are robust to such label noise and large implicit-feedback datasets remains unresolved. (3) Inductive generalization to new users/items: the present method is transductive—pruning is performed on the whole embedding matrix and does not naturally generalize to unseen users or items; designing pruning and sparse-embedding schemes that support inductive inference for new-coming users/items is an open problem. These limitations (cost of search, sensitivity to implicit-feedback noise, and lack of inductive extension) are explicitly identified as future work in the paper.
